primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Nephronophthisis is an autosomal recessive renal ciliopathy. Defects in nephrocystin and related ciliary proteins disrupt tubular epithelial signaling, producing impaired urinary concentration, chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis/fibrosis, tubular basement-membrane abnormalities, and later corticomedullary cyst formation.
vignette: A 12-year-old boy is evaluated for progressive fatigue and poor growth. For several years he has had marked thirst and frequent urination, including nocturia. Blood pressure is normal. Laboratory studies show normocytic anemia and elevated serum creatinine. Urinalysis shows minimal protein and no hematuria. Renal ultrasonography shows small-to-normal-sized echogenic kidneys with reduced corticomedullary differentiation and several small cysts at the corticomedullary junction.
lead: Dysfunction of which cellular structure most directly underlies this patient’s inherited kidney disease?
correct: Primary cilia of renal tubular epithelial cells
distractors: Type IV collagen network of the glomerular basement membrane
Nephrin-containing slit diaphragms between podocyte foot processes
Lysosomal cystine transporters in proximal tubular epithelial cells
Vasopressin V2 receptors on collecting-duct principal cells
distractor_notes: Type IV collagen defects cause Alport-spectrum glomerular basement-membrane disease with hematuria and often hearing/ocular findings, not the bland tubulointerstitial concentrating-defect pattern shown.
Nephrin/slit-diaphragm defects cause severe glomerular protein leakage, classically congenital nephrotic syndrome, rather than polyuria with little proteinuria and corticomedullary cysts.
Defective lysosomal cystine export causes cystinosis and proximal tubular Fanconi syndrome with generalized solute wasting, not the characteristic nephronophthisis phenotype.

V2-receptor dysfunction causes X-linked nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with impaired concentrating ability, but does not cause chronic tubulointerstitial fibrosis, anemia, progressive kidney failure, and corticomedullary cysts.
key_expl: This is nephronophthisis, an autosomal recessive ciliopathy and important inherited cause of kidney failure in children and young adults. Defects in NPHP genes impair proteins localized to primary cilia and related ciliary structures in renal tubular epithelial cells. The earliest clinical clue is often reduced urine-concentrating ability, producing polyuria and polydipsia. Progressive tubulointerstitial fibrosis causes anemia, growth impairment, and declining kidney function; imaging later may show small-to-normal kidneys with poor corticomedullary differentiation and corticomedullary cysts.
objective: Recognize nephronophthisis as an autosomal recessive renal ciliopathy causing an early concentrating defect followed by chronic tubulointerstitial fibrosis and corticomedullary cysts.
clues: child with chronic polyuria and polydipsia
normal blood pressure early in disease
